However, their performance suffers greatly when the training dataset is small, often less than 100 samples, due to a lack of diversity in the generated images which are essentially replicas of the training images. In response, we are working on an innovative approach that produces high-quality synthetic data from as few as 25 training samples per class. We began by enhancing the standard GAN model with two unique loss functions, known as the CLSSM and Minimum WHiteness L1 loss, which promote class-sensitive diversity in the synthetic data. In certain high-risk patient subgroups, failing to match them evenly across arms may also compromise the validity of the trial. As a result, they are often not thoroughly utilized in image synthesis research. In response to these limitations, a new evaluation platform called LIQAS has been developed. Unlike existing platforms, LIQAS integrates a range of widely-used quality metrics as well as similarity metrics based on color, spatial configurations, and semantic meanings. This platform showcases a comprehensive evaluation of quality metrics through a diverse set of image synthesis benchmarks. The platform is designed to support future research and is intended to be expanded into a broader assessment platform. Specifically, the site features comprehensive quality evaluation results of four spatial configuration evaluation methods, detailed analysis reports, and corresponding source codes. Moving forward, the platform aims to welcome more evaluation metrics and benchmarks from the image synthesis community, ultimately serving as a collaborative resource. In this article, an overview of the source and motivation behind LIQAS are explained, along with a description of the implementation details of the platform. This research investigates how to break these models into smaller parts and reuse existing models, applying part-sharing to end-to-end models for the first time. A combination of static and dynamic models is chosen for the initial candidate models.  A combination of teacher-student, distortion-relation, and entropy-based methods is proposed to determine the number of shared layers and neurons for each layer. A convergence acceleration method is proposed to determine the best training epoch for each layer.  When applied to the Distil-BERT, Distil-LSTM and UNET models, end-to-end models with 60% fewer parameters and 35% fewer operations show superior, state-of-the-art performance on speech, language and vision tasks, with weight burdens reduced by over 90%. Various methods for multiple projection spaces have been introduced, leading to different complete orthogonal factorizations of the mass matrix. Notably, all known approaches can be grouped under two categories: an energy-based approach and a mass-based approach. 

The energy-based approach views the constraint forces as energy multipliers, while the mass-based approach views them as power deliverers. In this paper, we will provide a systematic exploration of both viewpoints with an emphasis on the energy-based perspective, from which we derive new insights. 

Our generalized framework yields multiple types of reduced order models, not just static ones for stateless models, but also dynamic ones for state-dependent models. It should be noted that our dynamic models are not necessarily Portello-based, but rather are equivalent to those obtained by discretizing a variational integrator with a specific structure. 

Our theory is comprehensive and applies to a broad range of issues, particularly those related to issue-dependent projection spaces, where the constraint forces act non-uniformly. For underactuated bipedal walking, our reduced order models are dynamic, nonlinear, and C1-smooth, facilitating efficient numerical simulations of complex behaviors. 

In conclusion, our theoretical framework has the potential to be an overarching theory for reduced order modeling of underactuated mechanical systems with holonomic constraints, especially when actuation is limited. Our results on multiple types of reduced order models, issuing from a unified framework of CMD/PM, are expected to contribute significantly to OR, especially in the context of underactuated walking. 

Our work has been acknowledged through a recognized research grant from the NSF, supporting the work by the first author, while the second and third authors' work is supported by the startup funding provided by the Guangdong Province and Shandong Province, China, respectively.

This study serves as a foundation for investigating multi-variable and time-series data using a joint probability distribution. DGNNs are utilized to derive underlying cause, represented as world state, from visual observations in simulated robotic tasks. 

  Although DGNNs are disentangled, they are not specifically designed to capture temporal world state changes. To address this limitation, this paper presents temporal DGNNs (t-DGNNs), an extension of DGNNs that considers the progression of time. 

  To validate the performance of t-DGNNs, the approach is evaluated in two existing robotic datasets - predictive coding bayes (PCB) and robotic reach datasets - both created by Sironi (2020). The results of our experiments are available at https://github.com/mvrlab/temporal-dgnn. 

  The temporal extension of DGNNs is theoretically justified through the application of the joint generative network framework. The use of time series data does not breach the principles of disentanglement. Instead, the temporal extension serves as an aggregation of probabilistic world state models, weighing recent observations more heavily than historical ones. 

  To test the temporal DGNN, the approach is evaluated in two existing robotic datasets - PCB and robotic reach - both created by Sironi (2020). The results of our experiments are also compared to state-of-the-art temporal models, namely LSTM and TRPO, and future work involves utilizing t-DGNNs for predictive tasks in visual reach tasks. However, major graph learning frameworks have not yet incorporated operations that mirror matrix multiplication on discrete graphs, similar to the way vector and matrix operations are included in standard deep learning libraries. To address this gap, we have developed the graph matrix multiplication (GMM) operation, which provides a versatile way to apply arbitrary transformations to the matrix products of graph embeddings. Our operation allows users to customize the behavior of GMM by specifying a matrix that represents the set of all possible graph matrix products. This is in line with the approach taken by the matrix multiplication layer in TensorFlow. To optimize computational efficiency, we have developed a multi-threaded implementation of GMM that is capable of processing multiple graphs simultaneously. Experimental comparisons of the theoretical models developed in this research revealed significant performance variations based on the type of transformation, graph mixtures of degrees, and batch size. Notably, the inclusion of GMM led to the creation of a graph version of the Rezero residual connection, which resulted in the performance improvements of several other layers. This, in turn, enabled us to develop a rezero-residual network and the zerorezo-2 network, which achieved superior accuracy compared to the existing state-of-the-art models, such as the Graph-MLP P-SGN, on the benchmark datasets for unattributed, undirected social network analysis. Additionally, the graph matrix multiplication operation has the potential to be applied in numerous other graph learning tasks beyond social network analysis. Specifically, it is expected to be particularly beneficial for tasks that involve operating on the entire graph structure, such as predictive graph metrics, graph classification, link prediction, and operating on the adjacency matrix, as well as graph operations like graph pooling and graph normalisation. Further research will involve incorporating the operation of GMM into existing graph learning frameworks and making the theoretical models and implementation of the operation publicly available. This is expected to accelerate breakthroughs in the performance and understanding of graph learning methods. To facilitate this goal, we have developed a benchmark for evaluating the performance of graph learning models that utilize the operation of GMM. Besides their use in machine learning, the principles of the operation of GMM can also be applied in other fields, such as signal processing and physics, where graph data appears in its matrix form. Indeed, the operation of GMM might serve as a new paradigm for processing graph data much like the operation of vector and matrix products is a standard approach

However, these models are typically trained with uniformly structured data, whereas time series data can be better represented by accounting for the inherent irregularities and temporal variances within individual series. This paper introduces a novel method, Rooted Time Series Instance Embedding (RTIE), aiming to enhance time series instance representation and capture unique characteristics of individual series using the concept of rooted trees. RTIE uses a weighted average approach to compute mean and covariance matrices from time series values divided into irregular intervals, resulting in uniformly structured data for classification. RTIE is both efficient and effective, addressing the challenges posed by noisy data. Furthermore, we provide in-depth analysis and show its compatibility with contemporary time series classification models. Due to conservation laws, this interdependence is not necessarily resolved in quantum field descriptions, which can lead to silent violations of energy and momentum preservation.  To address these issues, we suggest looking at the entanglement in the context of the Dirac field and an electromagnetic field using two different frameworks: one that represents the external field using operators and another that uses classical quantities. First, we create a quantum blockchain based on the quantum authentication code of Brassard and Stern (BSBS), which enables verification of unvalid transactions and prevents quantum hackers from gaining control. Any attempt by a quantum hacker will be detected with a non-zero probability, allowing the blockchain to maintain its integrity even when attacked. In the quantum hacking scenario, our proposed quantum blockchain achieves a minimum success probability of $1/2^m$, where m represents the number of classical bits used for key generation via the BSBS code. Furthermore, our study investigates the quantum resilience of a blockchain when subjected to attacks, where the certified transaction is partially revealed, either in random or correlated fashion, by a quantum hacker using $N$ times of measurements. To counter such attacks, our design ensures that they can only be successful with a lower probability of $\frac{1/2^{m+N}}{1+{K \choose \frac{N}{2}}}$, significantly lower than the $1/2^m$ probability attainable by a classical hacker. Utilizing the binary tree of shared quantum bits, our proposed quantum blockchain can be easily extended to a parallelized version resistant to quantum hacking. In such a scenario, our design can withstand the attacks of a quantum hacker with a lower success probability of $\frac{1/2^{m+q}}{1+{K \pm \frac{q}{2} \choose \frac{q}{2}}}$, where $q$ represents the number of additional quantum bits shared via the binary tree, and $K$ is a parameter that allows us to trade off privacy and reliability. Our design provides an efficient and secure solution to allow blockchain operations to function in quantum environments. The feasibility of our design is confirmed by the significant reduction it achieves in broadcast communication overhead, amounting to at least an $O(Kq)$ times decrease in the classical messages needed to propagate on the binary tree, which traditionally requires $O(Kq)$ quantum messages to be quantum-resistant. The total overhead is expected to increase only by $O(Kq)$, largely due to the increased complexity of key generation, which remains secure with non-zero probability. Typically, these systems are treated as free-bouncing or elastic-bouncing systems when they reach their boundaries. However, we consider a more extensive class of systems in which the system can remain bound to the distribution for any energy level. We demonstrate that the scattering map for these systems exhibits a unique combination of properties from billiards and waves, including absolute continuity, differentiability, dependence on the system's speed, and essentially universal rigidity. We utilize the properties of hyperbolicity to establish the stability of linearly stable invariant planes and lines and show that certain conditions are necessary for the system's absolute stability. We establish the condition under which certain homogeneous, convex, centrally symmetric cones are invariant and show that specific homogeneous, symmetric bodies can generate purely elastic scattering. Moreover, we discover that a wide range of systems with a convex shape possess an absolutely continuous scattering map, assuming the system's coefficients change smoothly. If the system is as large as possible, it becomes maximally homogeneous, with a uniformly scattering map. We use the principles of geometric vision to provide intuitive explanations for these properties, and demonstrate the feasibility of numerically computing the absolute stability of scattering maps for intricate systems, including billiards and wave scattering. This study opens up new avenues for exploring the scattering maps of flat systems and their connections to the theory of dynamical systems. It also provides a potential connection to the field of power laws, as discussed in Section 6.0.2. Detailed scattering maps are now within reach for systems that were previously unsolvable, offering fresh approaches to data-driven research and the reconstruction of systems from limited data. This study paves the way for investigating the scattering maps of systems that are not flat, with a special focus on those with triangular shapes in various dimensions. This research also introduces the concept of geometrically encoding the scattering maps of systems, allowing us to derive new insights about their properties with minimal computational effort. As a result, it is now possible to design experimenter-friendly tools that help us gain a deeper understanding of the motion in complex environments. Current approaches to multi-step product recovery scenarios are scarce, and often they are based on simplified assumptions about opponents' strategies. This paper introduces a model for analyzing the movements of products through a series of recovery stages, where each step has multiple possible paths with associated costs and benefits. We formulate the recovery planning problem as a stochastic program with limited knowledge of the opponent's logic. To address limited knowledge, we explore two relaxed formulations: a deterministic equivalent and a conservative approximation. Our approach is validated by creating a decision-making model for a company that recovers and recycles electric vehicle batteries. We compare our methods with a exact model of the opponent's logic, and we find that the conservative approximation consistently yields a solution within a reasonable time frame, whereas the deterministic equivalent and semi-definite programming methods take significantly longer without guarantee of finding a solution as the number of decision variables increases. With the conservative approximation, we see clear patterns in the optimal resource allocation across different product flow paths, allowing for easier parameter analysis, regardless of the system size. This is a major advantage since examining the vast number of possible paths in the deterministic equivalent becomes impractical. With the growing number of companies participating in product recovery and recycling circuits, having an efficient and scalable model becomes increasingly crucial to make informed strategic decisions. By applying this approach to real-world data, we see how a company can optimize its recovery and recycling operations in response to the opponent's logic. Most recent works in the field have started exploring the utilization of the 2D lambda map to improve the detection of objects in the z-axis. As research continues, the application of the 2D lambda map has started to be replaced by the 3D lambda map which provides more accurate information and reduction of artificial interference. With the vast amount of 3D data increasing daily, the application of 3D deep learning technologies has now reached various fields including radio frequency, speech, EEG, microphonies, microscopy and electron microscopy data. This article aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the most recent deep learning advances in 3D smart sensing technologies. It starts with an introduction to the key technologies and methods used in this field, followed by the presentation of the most significant achievements through comparative analysis and discussion, and finally offers potential future research directions and challenges. One appendix is included which presents the most popular open-source deep learning frameworks for 3D data processing. This survey is intended to offer deep insights into the field and promote future innovations and research. It may serve as a valuable reference for researchers working in 3D deep learning areas and those interested in exploring this field further. Finally, it may inspire more young researchers to participate in 3D deep learning for smart wireless sensing technologies.

In our research, we utilize numerical simulations of turbulent magnetic fluid to simulate the behavior of magnetic fields in the solar atmosphere. To validate these simulations, we apply microscopic and macroscopic instability criteria to ensure the dynamic process was accurate. The results show that after a dynamic disturbance, the magnetic field components align in a similar pattern to 2-D flux operaters, and the stress they exert is directly related to solar spines and magnetic energy. Furthermore, the magnetic field curvature caused a decrease in the tension of horizontal magnetic fields and transverse Alfvén waves, allowing these waves to descend into the chromosphere carrying magnetic energy from the photosphere. We estimate the magnetic energy flux these waves carry to be transported into the chromosphere at a rate of 1100 erg/cm^2s. This study provides the first theoretical explanation for the independent formation of chromospheric magnetic field. It also confirms that Alfvén waves are capable of transporting energy from the photosphere to the chromosphere, shedding light on the heating mechanism of the chromosphere. Conversely, it is also possible that the chromosphere could be placed under pressure by Alfvén waves and magnetic energy from the photosphere for an extended period of time. These findings support the notion that the chromosphere is dynamically driven by both the magnetic field and Alfvén waves. The high flux of magnetic energy from the photosphere to the chromosphere is consistent with the required energy to maintain the thermodynamic balance of the chromosphere and possibly its fine structure. These findings also confirm that magnetic field tension is responsible for the pressure in the chromosphere. This study's results will be the subject of a forthcoming paper discussing wave dynamics. We have applied similar analysis to investigate the relationship between the chromosphere and corona. In this case, the required flux of magnetic energy from the chromosphere to the corona is several orders of magnitude higher than what is required for the photosphere to the chromosphere, indicating that the chromosphere is not sufficient to power the coronal heating and the solar atmosphere needs to be redefined. These findings also suggest that the solar atmosphere can no longer be regarded as consisting of distinct layers but must be viewed as a continuous entity. In this sense, the chromosphere is not capable of maintaining its thermodynamic balance on its own but relies on a more extensive thermal and dynamic regime. We will examine these phenomena not only from a mathematical perspective but also from the views of physics and biology. Isometric inclusions of manifolds and group actions will be presented as primary sources for the generation of isospectral pairs of operators. We will analyze the dependence of isospectral pairs on the group action, especially in cases involving finite groups, and explore their connections to other mathematical concepts, such as the Burnside's folk theorem for finite groups, symmetric spaces, and algebraic groups. In addition, this article will provide an overview of the prevalence of isospectral pairs in the context of Lie groups and their connection to other Lie groups, especially simple Lie groups. We will also examine the occurrence and significance of isospectral pairs in well-known geometric spaces, such as the Poincaré sphere, Chen's orbifolds, and symmetric spaces related to ADE-type Lie algebras, as well as the more general Gorenstein gradient Schubert variety. Isospectral pairs in the context of algebraic groups are closely related to another topic in this article: pairs of operators on complex algebraic tori admitting the action of the multiplicative group. We will present the connection between these isospectral pairs and nilpotent cones of certain Lie algebras associated with ADE-type. We will also provide an overview of the study of ordinary and hyperbolic differential operators on the hyperbolic plane and identify the key results discovered recently. In addition, this article presents several open problems. For instance, classifying isospectral pairs of ordinary and hyperless differential operators on a compact, curved space remains an unsolved issue, especially on spaces that are not analytically separable. Another area that lacks a comprehensive solution is the characterization of isospectral pairs of ordinary and hyperbolic differential operators on a torus with various group actions. Lastly, this article poses the question: what types of non-Abelian groups feature isospectral pairs of ordinary and hyperbolic differential operators on a compact, curved space? "Modern Developments in Variable Sea Level" and delves into the practical implications of predicting sea level with the aid of statistical and machine learning methods. The discussion is centered around the distinct phases within the sea level prediction task, assessing the feasibility of incorporating machine learning in each phase based on an examination of the current state-of-the-art. The analysis reveals substantial opportunities for the integration of machine learning methods to enhance the initial signal identification and understanding of physical processes governing the sea level, as well as in the estimation phase, particularly with the increasing availability of remote sensing data. However, we find limited potential for the application of machine learning in the warning phase due to the prevalence of traditional methods that prioritize simplicity over efficiency. Ultimately, we outline potential future research pathways within the sea level prediction domain. The corresponding implementation of deep learning models can significantly reduce computational burdens when processing data from remote sensing sources, facilitating the adoption of machine learning methods in the estimation phase. has recently exploded with diverse models being proposed to tackle various tasks, yet multiple studies aim to specific areas of the vast graph domain. Consequently, no single benchmark "covers the entire landscape." In an effort to address this, a new set of tasks - lastly selected through public poll - are introduced within the OGNI framework. By incorporating 13 tasks, the OGNI framework seeks to address a critical challenge in the GNN field: training models on vast, real-world graph datasets in an effort to achieve state-of-the-art performance across a wide array of possible graph transformations. By promoting the development of general, robust GNN models capable of performing well across a broad spectrum of graph manipulations, the OGNI framework aims to address an often-overlooked area of the GNN topic: the transfer learning phenomenon. In this paper, we present the OGNI framework, accompanied by initial experiments designed to measure the impact of existing GNN models on specific graph transformations. We also discuss and identify potential avenues for improving the underlying graph learning dynamics. Ultimately, the OGNI framework serves as a starting point for further research, intended to stimulate the development of a unified theory of the GNN topic: the transfer learning phenomenon. We present an open-source implementation of the framework at https://github.com/simonmellem/OGNI.

In this study, we introduce a novel approach to assess a model's capacity for reasoning over multiple answer choices. We have compiled a large dataset consisting of more than 378,000 question-answer pairs from the General Knowledge Quiz dataset, along with their corresponding annotations of primitively interpreted meaning. It is often challenging to accurately predict how information flows and is managed within such networks, particularly in large sizes. However, processing time is typically directly related to the network's size. Contrary to expectations, our study reveals that processing time in these systems for specific, predefined tasks exhibits a sublinear relationship with the network size. This unexpected sublinear behavior is a result of the consolidation of correlations in the network, stemming from the way information is managed. However, this effect only occurs when the network's properties are dynamically adjusted and can no longer be accounted for by static statistical models. Our findings involve simulations of a basic information management system where particles periodically send messages to determine the current network state. Large networks exhibit a sublinear relationship between processing time and network size, characterized by the parameter t, with processing time being proportional to t times the cube root of the network size. The sublinear behavior is further confirmed through analytical calculations and experiments on random networks, demonstrating that the time required to process information is directly influenced by the extent of internal correlations within the network, even when the network is large. This study has significant implications for understanding complex systems where information management plays a crucial role, for example, belief update in social networks, traffic flow, and cellular signal processing. It also opens up new avenues of research, particularly the design of efficient algorithms for managing information in complex systems, and may ultimately lead to a deeper understanding of the general principles governing the dynamics of massive information networks. Our work also has the potential to inspire new experimental studies focusing on the relationships between spatial and temporal patterns in chemical systems equipped with feedback mechanisms, known as cheminformatics. Similarly, prioritizing defences that curtail user access to sensitive data also yields minimal volume loss with a high confidence rate. This work explores relationships between the quantum complexity of Boolean functions and their accessibility on quantum computers via measurement techniques. It introduces a crucial aspect: the quantum control of Boolean functions, which explains how complex a quantum circuit must be to compute a function through measurements. For example, we demonstrate that a function with quantum complexity of $d$ can be computed by a quantum circuit of length $d^2$, and that a function with classical complexity of $d$ and quantum complexity greater than $d^2$ is resistant to certain common quantum attacks. Further, we propose a new quantum complexity measure, the quantum spectral complexity, which is directly connected to the quantum control of Boolean functions through measurements. Finally, we provide evidence that the quantum spectral complexity of a function can be efficiently estimated by a quantum circuit of length $n$, where $n$ is the number of variables in the function. This research outputs a database containing the spectral complexities of over 16,000 unique Boolean functions, along with corresponding quantum control values for functions defined by size $n\leq 20$. Moreover, for functions with $n\leq 12$, we present a path towards computing the quantum control value via a method that simulates the quantum complexity of superpositions of Boolean functions. Lastly, for functions with $n\leq 5$, we present exact results for the quantum control value, obtained via the precomputing process that yielded the database. Researchers investigated this time required for generating the Bell pair by analyzing the rate at which photons emerge from interacting atoms after being hit with incredibly powerful light pulses containing millions of photons. They discovered that around five trillion collisions are needed to create the Bell pair, which takes place in approximately 10 picoseconds, following the beginning of the strong light pulse interaction. Notably, this time constant matches the light speed limit and is consistent with the time it takes for entropy to form in a system. They also found that the entropy of the scattered light follows a specific pattern and amounts to the maximum possible value. This pattern consists of the scattering of atoms into either a superposition of two or no states, indicating distinct phases of the light pulse interaction. Two key methods are proposed to optimize the creation of the Bell pair, consisting of utilizing a sequence of light pulses or enhancing the light interaction with the atoms. Utilizing two sequential pulses boosts the production rate, while interacting the light with the atoms more efficiently can do the same. Ultimately, it is anticipated that the proposed methods will lead to the development of faster entangling protocols. Furthermore, it is hoped that the proposed methods will lead to the identification of new ways to utilize entangled particles more effectively in quantum information technologies. cosmic rays are likely to be cosmically detected near future facilities like the ELISe experiment, which will be located on the International Space Station and capable of observing particle air showers with an approximately 350 km altitude. Understanding the composition of these cosmic rays and their energy spectrum relies on accurately interpreting observations of particle air showers. This paper proposes a model-based fitting method to extract the primary particle information from time-dependent cosmic ray data. The model assumes that either the mass or the energy of primary cosmic rays changes over time, with the rate of change in mass being linear or the rate of change in energy being constant. Analyzing synthetic data, we found that our approach allows for precise recovery of the primary parameters, with an root mean square error of approximately 3% for a sample size of 1000 experiments. Furthermore, we investigated how various levels of statistical noise influence our results, with the worst-case scenario producing an rmse of around 9%. To prepare for real-world observations, we used synthetic experiments mimicking the performance of ELISe's Wilson-Cambridge time projection chambers, incorporating electron cloud effects and multiple scattering. Our model-based fitting method is a valuable tool that will help to shed light on the evolution of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays over time. The associated code is available at https://github.com/supermoe/ELISe-UCR-analysis, with the simulated data used in this study generated using the UCR simulation framework at https://github.com/supermoe/UCR-code.

This research considers a simplified interaction to provide general insights into the characteristics of the stochastic gravitational-wave background in more complex scenarios. As a concrete application, we investigate the potential detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background generated by the spin-independent interactions of ultra-light vector bosons with electrons. Our study reveals that such a light boson with a mass range of $10^{-20}-10^{-18}$ GeV can be identified by combining measurements from LIGO and Advanced Virgo detectors with a judicious data selection strategy. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system disturbances and subtle environmental changes. Designing handcrafted features can also restrict a model's ability to automatically learn relevant features. Clarifying the generalizability of DNNs in channel-based localization is essential for their practical application. In this research, we investigate the channel under diverse system conditions. We also compare the performance of a decision-level method using existing CSI to an alternative approach, which utilizes joint channel features to train a single, unified model. Our analysis reveals that the second approach yields superior results and better generalization capabilities. We also illustrate that the channel prediction performance of DNNs can provide insight into the system localization accuracy. The practical implications of our findings are verified through experiments conducted indoors and outdoors. Our research provides fundamental training and evaluation guidelines for DNN-based channel-based localization, which will facilitate the practical application of this technology. By establishing a degree-based inequality for these zeta functions, we demonstrate their convergence on a specific region of the complex plane. Additionally, a boundary phenomenon is identified, along with a specific asymptotic behavior verified for functions associated with arbitrarily small perturbations of the Euclidean tensor operator. Crucial to these findings are two key inequalities, the first of which relates to the Laplace-Beltrami operator with Dirichlet boundary conditions, while the second concerns the Laplace-Beltrami operator with Neumann boundary conditions. Both inequalities were found to be uncertain for positive curvature. This discovery led us to the formulation of the Duflo-Hermann-Rosenmüller zeta functions as derivatives of the locally symmetric zeta functions at s=1. This identification enabled us to establish the Riemann Hypothesis for functions associated with arbitrarily small perturbations of the Euclidean tensor operator. However, we could not confirm the Riemann Hypothesis for functions related to positively curved polyhedra. Nonetheless, the findings highlight the Duflo-Hermann-Rosenmüller zeta functions as relevant objects of study in the field. This investigation was made possible through the Delaunay-Isaacs lemma, which provided the link between these zeta functions and the locally symmetric zeta functions. Moreover, the central role of maximally symmetric spaces in the analysis paved the way for a deeper exploration of these functions, which may ultimately lead to a confirmation of the Riemann Hypothesis for positively curved compact polyhedra. The conclusions presented here serve as a foundation for future research initiatives. asks whether the area under the influence curve can be quantified when the attacker's objective is not directly measurable. Answering this query would enable the creation of adversarial samples under controlled constraints even when the attacker's goals are unclear. To address this challenge, we frame the influence curve as a dual problem of a convex optimization task and formulate a relaxation of this optimization. This relaxation enables us to derive an upper bound for the area under the influence curve, although this bound does not serve as a measure for all possible adversaries. We then introduce two additional optimization problems, one of which yields a tighter lower bound and the other a tighter upper bound for the measure in question. We provide specific algorithms to solve these problems in specific contexts, specifically for neural networks that utilize the ReLU activation function and have a parameter update rule based on gradient descent. In line with our results on relaxations, we perform an extensive analysis of different possible adversaries, deriving the influence curve when the attacker's objective is to minimize specific loss functions, including the cross-entropy loss and the squared loss. To validate our theoretical findings, we carry out an experimental evaluation of their practical usefulness, showing that our analysis can be employed by data owners to devise effective defensive strategies, especially when dealing with adversarial attacks that are not motivated by a specific objective function. Our study also provides a practical approach for estimating the influence curve even in scenarios with an unbounded set of possible adversaries. This can help to accelerate research in several machine learning subfields by accounting for the influence curve in theoretical analyses and to improve the robustness of neural networks in practice. Consequently, this work can serve as a foundation for subsequent studies that utilize our analysis to devise new countermeasures against adversarial attacks. Our analysis can also be utilized to facilitate a more realistic training of neural networks that are resilient to such attacks, especially when the attacker's objective is to minimize specific loss functions, including the cross-entropy loss and the squared loss. Moreover, the defense strategies that correspond to our tight upper bounds on the measure have the advantage of being easily adaptable to different architectures of the neural network, whether these are based on ReLU or have a more complex piecewise-linear activation function, such as that of ReLU++ or xelu. Importantly, the general framework of the analysis, which enables the derivation of a influence curve that accounts for various possible adversaries, can be extended to cover a variety of different attack models, thus providing a useful framework for future research in the field of adversarial machine learning. technology has the potential to transform the integration of renewable energy in transportation into the power grid, ensuring that vehicles act as reliable energy storage systems to mitigate the unpredictability of renewable energy sources. Despite this promise, the complexity of electrical systems on modern vehicles makes it difficult to design and simplify the control systems for individual vehicles. Neural Networks, have the capability to quantify uncertainty in their predictions by modeling noise in training labels. By incorporating these noise models, BNNs can overcome data selection biases present in traditional training label assumptions. Despite this advantage, designing an optimal noise model proving that it converges to the true distribution remains challenging, particularly for complex datasets. This study examines a specific Bayesian Neural Network set up commonly used in computer vision tasks, exploring its properties when trained with images. The analysis shows that assuming a simple independent bivariate distribution for label noise, despite its complexity, does converge to the true image distribution for certain BNN set ups commonly used in computer vision tasks. This result provides a solid foundation for quantitative uncertainty analysis in computer vision tasks and encourages further research in applying theoretical quantitative methods to visual data. This study builds upon previous work, improving the theoretical range of the bivariate noise model and expanding it to accommodate practical training settings featuring multiple labels. The theoretical findings are further supported by numerical experiments demonstrating the effects of incorrectly assumed noise models. To demonstrate this, we present a scenario where the demon's ability to generate power depends on its inability to tap into a supplementary, heat-bath-like degree of freedom. While the existing information held by the demon is sufficient to prevent ordinary heat transfer, this additional information source must be accessed to allow the demon to extract work efficiently from the system. However, doing so incurs a substantial cost: a measurable, physically observable effect that serves as a realization of Landauer's principle in a single process, effectively quantifies the cost of eliminating unwanted information. Moreover, we show that this single step is part of a broader sequence of operations that realizes another long-debated concept, the Maxwell demon's optimal information extraction process, recently defined by Levitin and Lebowitz. Notably, we prove that this process, when considered in its entirety, still reflects a physical manifestation of Landauer's principle, illustrating a hidden yet explicit form of information dynamics. In effect, the optimal demon still stands as a model where the cost of information extraction by a second law-based maximal demon is equal to $\beta\log_2 2$. Recently, this cost has been linked to a change in system entropy by Lebowitz and Ng in an unrelated context. Here, we show, with varying temperatures, and with a mixed initial state, that this change in system entropy corresponds to the emerging physical entropy of the third, key degree of freedom governing the demon's optimal operations. Additionally, we derive the conditions under which the demon can still achieve maximal information extraction while minimizing the emerging physical entropy of the third degree of freedom. Overall, our work serves as a physical realization of recent advances in the theoretical understanding of Maxwell's demon, as detailed in a companion study that also generalizes the results to all thermodynamic processes, revealing a hidden yet explicit form of the second law, where the emerging physical entropy of a certain, potentially an infinite number of degrees of freedom ($S_{\text{phys}}$) becomes a fundamental thermodynamic potential. consisting of ferromagnetic, semiconducting Ca$_3$Li$_2$Fe$_6$Te$_4$, a compound featuring a unique cluster magnetic structure. Upon cooling, the compound exhibits a collossal specific heat peak at its Curie temperature of approximately 340 K, indicative of the individual magnetic cluster magnetization process. Magnetic clusters comprising five coupled Fe$^{2+}$ spins, arranged in an irregular tetrahedron with no symmetry elements, are responsible for this phenomenon. This phenomenon is explained by a single-ion origin known as the untuned Néel mechanism. This property can be formulated as: for every statement A of a certain language, there exists another statement B, such that the combination of A and B is consistent. This property has been given distinct names in separate logics, such as the Craig interpolation theorem for classical logic, the interpolation theorem for modal logic, the Haken theorem for intuitionistic logic, and others. Our work focuses on extending the interpolation theorem to contexts that involve nested names for classes. These extensions have been successfully applied to logics with nested frameworks, such as second-order logic and bi-modal logic. However, the interpolation theorem does not extend smoothly to logics with nested operators, like modal logic with operators that affect multiple levels. An exception is the proof process known as cut-elimination, which can provide insight into interpreting the interpolation theorem. This paper explores the generalization of the interpolation theorem to logic systems with nested names for classes, using the cut-free proof process as a guiding framework. Similar to classical logic, we suspect that the generalization of the interpolation theorem should be achievable in contexts with a certain linear structure, like the proof process known as linear logic with nested operators. This is supported by the existing linear logic theorem known as the "Sellinger theorem." However, our current work only addresses non-commutative linear logic without the "!'' operator, and we have discovered a new proof for this that uses the concept of uniform interpolation in addition to the cut-elimination theorem, and we have also shown that this proof is adaptable to a broader class of linear logics. An extension of our work on linear logics may also be applied to other linear structures, such as virtual logic and quantalic logic, and we have also mentioned the potential for adding operators that affect multiple levels to separate modal logics while still preserving the interpolation theorem. Existing solutions often simplify such complex graphs into simpler forms or convert them into unweighted, undirected networks. Despite this common practice, we don't have a clear understanding of when and how this transformation impacts learning outcomes. This paper provides a theoretical framework to study the effects of edge simplification by examining the properties of linear graph neural networks. Our findings reveal that simplifying edge directions can lead to complete edge loss in the resulting graph, whereas modifying or dropping edge weights may result in a network where node features cannot be learned. This suggests that, in certain scenarios, preserving edge directions is more critical than preserving edge weights when working with neural networks. This paper's contributions offer a deeper understanding of when edge modification or loss is acceptable when using linear graph neural networks. These findings also shed light on the requirements for training graph neural networks, particularly with regard to consistency with the underlying target graph, even when the network's parameters are learned from a graph that differs in edge density or weight distribution. Our theoretical discoveries are accompanied by empirical studies of simple graph operations, along with a new algorithm for graph weight normalization, WeightSpaceTransform. The latter is demonstrated to be more robust than other normalization techniques, especially in the context of linear graph neural networks. Finally, this paper proposes several potential areas for expansion, including the extension of this work to linear graph convolutional networks and the exploration of new graph neural network training paradigms that are compatible with edge modifications. This research offers a fundamental understanding of graph neural network training and outlines necessary conditions for transforming graph structures without compromising learning outcomes. Additionally, our WeightSpaceTransform method demonstrates the importance of carefully selecting the new weight space for graph neural network training. From a computational perspective, our analysis focuses on the effects of simplifying graph structures, particularly the loss of edges. This study could be extended by modeling more complex transformations between graph types, such as between directed simple graphs and weighted undirected graphs. Conversely, this research may be generalized to other graph transformation paradigms by applying and testing the proposed conditions. Moreover, the algorithmic aspects of this work could be expanded by developing new graph normalization methods that preserve the distribution of edge weights. Lastly, this research offers a comprehensive framework for analyzing other graph transformation paradigms, such as graph edge direction changes, and provides the potential for new insights and applications to emerge. Traditional reliability assessment of road networks, including finding the shortest path with a specific survival probability, can be cumbersome due to the need for frequent iterations. Recent frameworks offering real-time reliability analysis involve dividing populations into segments based on their service level requirements and employing Monte Carlo simulation to project demand. However, these frameworks struggle to keep up with the frequency of queries and the expanding road networks, causing delays in responding to emerging events. Scheduling for real-time traffic, such as serving packets immediately or within known wait times, necessitates knowledge of individual flow transforms to guarantee specified performance targets.  Unknown flow transforms pose a significant challenge, leading researchers to propose various methods for estimating this unknown variable.  Recent studies have shown that statistical properties of served packets can be utilized to estimate the flow transform, and this work further explores the use of relative indices, such as the jitter or free delay, for transform estimation. We derive the equilibrium phase structure, thermodynamic properties, and phase transitions of these black holes, including their critical behavior. We compare the thermodynamic properties of these black holes with those of the Maxwell scalar-black hole system and find that they exhibit similar behavior. The difficulty in achieving this goal often stems from the limited spatial information contained within single-channel audio feeds. In order to improve sound source localization in the context of video conferencing, we investigated the utilization of multiple audio channels for 3D localization purposes. Given that common use cases already provide 2nd order spatial cues in the form of stereo or multi-channel audio, we focused our analysis on the performance of 2nd order localization under the influence of common real-world background noises. In this context, our research involves the creation of a new dataset that combines previously existing multi-channel audio data with corresponding room simulation results, enabling the training of a model that can improve 2D audio localization accuracy by approximately 11.3%. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrated that the proposed method exhibits diminished sensitivity to background noise, with a $6.1\%$ or $2.1\%$ decrease in 3D localization error for single- or 2nd order spatial cue conditions, respectively. The outcomes of this study suggest that the technique can be applied in the realm of video conferencing for the purpose of 3D audio localization, in addition to being a suitable model-conditional approach for the problem of single-channel audio localization. The corresponding code and dataset can be accessed at: https://github.com/kuoshin/2nd-order-loc.git. In accordance with the research's results, a novel method for refining 2nd order localization results was developed and implemented, in addition to which a comparative analysis was performed under the influence of beamforming filters, in addition to which the spatial grid resolution was discovered to significantly influence the localization's overall localization error performance. In an effort to further decrease 3D localization error, particularly for the case of single-channel audio, our research also includes the development of a novel localization model that achieves enhanced localization results in comparison to the existing benchmark tools. In contrast to existing model-conditional approaches for single-channel audio localization, the newly introduced model possesses the unique attribute of being trainable without the necessity for explicit pitch estimation, in addition to which the new approach demonstrates on-average 3D localization error improvements of $4.8\%$ or $3.0\%$ over the WaveLocation and ALFRED methods when tested on test-clean or test-reverberant conditions, respectively. We propose a method of hierarchical access where patients' consent is obtained from distinct entities for the initial request, and these consent decisions are later used to approve subsequent requests in a hierarchical structure. We also investigate how our approach can accommodate time-sensitive and location-specific requests while maintaining an acceptable level of computational efficiency. The results demonstrate that our framework offers substantial support for the management of EHR access requests while also showcasing notable efficiency compared to existing solutions. Low computational overhead is achieved with our approach requiring only four cryptographic computations and zero interactions with external entities, in addition to verifying external requests five times and constructing a key derivation function once. We also saw a 44% decrease in response latency in our performance testing and a 43% improvement in energy consumption, when compared to the best-optimized solution available. Using real spacecraft data, it's been found that UV-CAPS can consistently operate at a time resolution of less than 1.6 seconds across its entire operating wavelength range. This successful characterization is an important achievement for the development of UV-CAPS and Ariel, and will be essential for the analysis of future observations. Our final analysis shows that UV-CAPS can accurately reproduce time series data from step change tests, and that its noise levels are consistent across different frequencies of observation. This paper includes the full experimental design of the tests carried out, and is the first of two papers related to this characterization, the second of which will focus on the frequency response of UV-CAPS. This paper explores an innovative method to design adversarial patches that are compatible with various types of sensors, using a patch-centered approach that determines an optimal patch shape. When applied to different sensor domains, our approach achieved the highest success rate so far, outperforming previous studies. This research has no access restrictions and the source code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/lincodeer/SensorAdversarialPatches.git
  Adversarial patch attacks that craft the physical world's malicious debris have received considerable attention lately. Despite existing research, effectively creating such patches remains challenging, especially when dealing with single sensor inputs in industrial settings. To overcome this, our approach designs low-cost, sensor-friendly adversarial patches. By utilizing a patch encoder, we determine an optimal patch shape that's compatible with various sensors. When applied to different sensor domains, our approach achieved the highest success rate so far, outperforming previous studies. This research has no access restrictions and the source code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/lincodeer/SensorAdversarialPatches.git

We developed a non-orthogonal error-correcting phase-matching QKD protocol that allows for real-time communication. In this protocol, the private key generation process involves a main channel and two side channels. A set of phase-matching keys from the main channel are randomly divided into two parts and two side channel keys are generated through independent measurements. Side channel keys are combined with main channel keys via exclusive or operation and the final key is generated through threshold decoding. We conducted an experimental study of this protocol and evaluated its security using a real-time measurement system. The results confirmed the security of this protocol against the main channel attack, indicating a promising solution for real-time QKD applications. The protocol's implementation also offers a higher communication efficiency than traditional phase-matching QKD. We successfully achieved a high communication speed of 6.56 Mbps at a distance of 25km. This protocol's property of side channel post-selecting can achieve a high communication speed of 55.56 Mbps but at the risk of security vulnerability to code hacking. We proposed a counter-measure to mitigate this vulnerability and concluded that the main limitation to increasing communication speed lies in the light source rather than the property of side channel post-selecting. We also conducted a comparison of this protocol with other QKD protocols and verified its superiority in terms of communication efficiency. Further analysis into the counter-measure is necessary to determine its effectiveness in practice. The potential side channel attack should be further investigated to reduce reliance on post-selecting and facilitate real-time QKD communication as well as improve security against attacks. The development of a fast and secure real-time QKD system is poised to drive advancements in this field. Finally, the possibility of employing multiple light sources could further maximize communication efficiency and enable the development of a fast and secure real-time QKD system. The potential existence of the noisiness loophole remains to be determined and needs further research in this field. To address this need, we have developed a novel, hardware-based system for detecting malicious code at the instruction fetch stage, utilizing dynamic instruction mixing.  This system works by generating a diverse set of short, merged instructions from incoming fetch requests and then processing them in the Memory (MA) unit to determine non-emulative behavior.  This processing involves either a comparison with expected but malicious results in the Comparison (C) unit, or an execution of the merged instructions in the Emulation (EM) unit to identify self-modifying code.  Our proposed architecture, termed MC-MA, is a tri-modal system that combines these components to effectively distinguish legitimate instructions from malicious ones.  By implementing MC-MA using digital logic, we have observed a maximum of 6.66% area increase and 11.16% energy reduction compared to existing solutions, showcasing its feasibility.  To accommodate only analog processing within MC-MA, we have developed an analog version of this system, termed MC-AnA.  This can be implemented using simple analog circuits, yielding a significant reduction of 61.2% and 68.9% in power consumption and area, respectively, when compared to the original digital design.  Additionally, these analog solutions offer notable improvements in energy efficiency and area complexity compared to existing analog solutions, making them superior options.  Furthermore, both the digital and analog versions of MC-MA exhibit high security and accuracy metrics, demonstrating their effectiveness in detecting malicious attacks.  To summarize, MC-MA represents a significant advancement in hardware-based security systems, offering high detection accuracy and Malware Coverage Ratio (MCR) values, as well as minimal area and power consumption.  This is achieved through the design of digital and analog detection models, the former of which can be effectively realized using CMOS technology, and the latter of which benefits from analog computation for energy efficiency but incurs complexity in reading output results.  To overcome this challenge, future research could focus on developing a sensing circuit for analog-based MC-MA similar to those already used in existing analog security systems.  To promote the design of analog detection models, we have provided comprehensive SPICE models and tested the proposed MC-MA architecture using an analog simulator, validating its operation and efficiency. deep learning in bioinformatics, there is a significant shortage of suitable large-scale medical image datasets. This missing link necessarily leads to the pursuit of cost-effective data augmentation methods that can expand training datasets while maintaining their underlying data quality. Such an approach has been widely adopted in the field of medical image processing. In deep learning context, medical image augmentation is primarily achieved through manipulation of image attributes including spatial, rotation, and intensity. However, this approach may not be sufficient due to the inherent lack of representativeness in handling rare medical conditions, a challenge inherent in all augmentation techniques. 
   The emergence of medical virtual reality technologies has presented new avenues for medical training, treatment, and patient care. As the adoption of deep learning in medical virtual reality accelerates, creating realistic virtual patients plays a crucial role in advancing MRgFODF-based automated radiogenomics. However, designing and optimizing 3D virtual patients poses significant difficulties due to the intricate link between anatomical structures and tissues. This paper proposes the adoption of multimodal augmentation techniques to expand existing white matter lesion simulation methods, showcasing their efficacy in briding the gap between rare and common conditions, a concern shared by most existing augmentation methods. Moreover, this technique has the potential to enhance the accuracy of supervised learning models used in radiogenomics. It is demonstrated through experiments that the proposed method can successfully create a diverse and realistic database of virtual patients from a relatively small-scale ground truth dataset. This is achieved without further annotating the ground truth by a medical expert. It is notable that the proposed method is readily available for immediate use. It is envisioned that this method can facilitate the development of large-scale medical image databases, a crucial requirement for building deep learning models, especially in the application of medical genomics and machine learning. The source code is available at: https://github.com/mandylabs/MultiModalAugmentation.

$k$-Satisfiability ($k$-SAT) problem consists of a formula with exactly $k$ distinct logical operations (either AND or OR) being applied over a set of $n$ variables. It is known that each $k$-SAT instance has exactly $2^n$ ground truth assignments.

  Define the Stable Number of a $k$-SAT instance $I$, denoted by $\sigma_I(n)$, as the minimum number of variables needed to uniquely identify $I$ from its subset with $n$ variables.

  This paper provides an upper limit on $\sigma_I(n)$ for random $k$-SAT instances. The upper bound decreases as more information about the instance becomes available.

  Specifically, when no information is known about the instance, the upper bound on $\sigma_I(n)$ for random $k$-SAT is of the order $\mathcal{O}(n \log k)$.

  When the instance is known to be unsatisfiable, the upper bound on $\mathcal{H}_I(n)$, where $\mathcal{H}_I(n)$ denotes the minimum number of variables needed to uniquely identify all unsatisfiable subsets of $I$, is of the order $\mathcal{O}(n \log k)$.

  When a resolution refutation of the instance is known, the upper bound on $\sigma_I(n)$ is of the order $\mathcal{O}(n \log \log k)$.

  These upper bounds are derived by establishing a probabilistic model for random $k$-SAT instances.

  These findings are significant as they indicate that, even for unsatisfiable random $k$-SAT instances, the minimum number of variables needed to uniquely identify them grows logarithmically with the number of variables.

  Moreover, the upper bounds imply that solving $(k-1)$-SAT exactly in polynomial time would have important implications for solving $k$-SAT. Thus, the results provide further evidence for the difficulty of solving $k$-SAT. Furthermore, the results provide an explanation for why, in practice, it is possible to solve randomly generated $k$-SAT instances of up to 4096 variables within a reasonable time frame. The models developed for upper bounding $\sigma_I(n)$ may be useful for designing new algorithms for solving $k$-SAT. Additionally, the models can be used for studying properties of resolution, a refutationally complete theorem prover for $k$-SAT. In a separate study,

This phenomenon has sparked curiosity among mathematicians and physicists, who are seeking a quantitative understanding of this effect. In our research, we propose a statistical model that captures how communication and random collaboration impact collective problem-solving capabilities. This model, based on an erasure process of random polymers, is experimentally verified using simulations of a cooperative task completed by homogeneous and heterogeneous teams. The results show that, as predicted by our theory, more diverse teams are likely to excel in problem-solving, albeit only up to a point, after which team performance does not continue to improve. Importantly, our research provides a framework for extracting specific parameters from experimental data that can be linked to underlying physical properties, such as the movement of molecules, as well as a general understanding of the optimal diversity range. This knowledge could have far-reaching applications, extending beyond the specific context of our experiments, which were conducted with agents completing a daily survival task. The insights from our research could be applied to other real-world challenges, including disease transmission, traffic flow, and the spread of information, to name a few. Ultimately, our findings serve as a foundation for future investigations into diversity effects in complex systems. From a practical standpoint, our research provides a simple method for experimentally determining the optimal range of diversity in achieving collective efficiency. A new AI framework is now available to analyze electron beam treatment plans and help optimize brain radiotherapy treatments. This novel AI framework automatically extracts key treatment parameters, including the treatment's volume, dose, and number of treatment sessions, as well as treatment outcomes, directly from the images used to plan the treatment. This reduces the risk of human errors previously encountered in manual data collection. The AI framework's accuracy was tested on 249 actual brain radiotherapy plans. Compared to the original treatment parameters documented by doctors, the AI-driven analysis matched them with less than 1% difference. This study's results show that its "end-to-end" method is both reliable and efficient. When applied to clinical trials, the AI-driven analysis of electron beam treatment plans can automatically compile treatment data to inform research questions. This is particularly beneficial in studies comparing different treatment options, where traditional methods involve manually collecting and organizing the data from the images used to plan the treatments. The AI-driven analysis can significantly reduce the time and resources required for such studies. Using the AI framework automatically Compiles the treatment data for various research questions. This is illustrated by applying the AI-driven analysis to a specific study on active implantable devices, where the AI-generated treatment parameters revealed that certain treatments were associated with treatment outcomes. However, it is crucial to note that the AI-driven analysis, although accurate and efficient, can only extract information available in the images used to plan the treatments. Therefore, the research findings using the AI-driven analysis rely heavily on the accuracy of these images and the treatment plans documented by doctors. The implementation of the AI-driven analysis is open-source, providing a foundation for further discussions on its applications and limitations. Based on the results of this study, the authors recommend promoting the use of AI in clinical trials involving the comparison of different treatment options, especially those involving radiotherapy. This article presents a new ensemble-based verification method for verifying the dynamics of mean climate trends in model simulations, especially where the underlying observation error structures are unknown. approach to protect machine learning models against data-poisoning attacks, where the model is trained on artificially created data sets that are expected to be resistant to manipulation. At the core of the proposal is the hypothesis that successful attacks on learning models are rare events dependent on specific conditions, suggesting that large numbers of attack scenarios can be prevented if certain characteristics can be identified. Based on this idea, two methods have been developed to create these preventive scenarios, leading to an improved training regime of the model, thereby increasing its robustness to potential poisonings. Experiments using the well-known MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets have shown substantial performance gains, with up to a 70-fold reduction in the cost associated with detecting poisonings, along with a 50-fold decrease in the accuracy of which-influence attacks, as well as improved resilience to such attacks. Notably, this synthesis-based defense is compatible with existing techniques and can be used in conjunction with established defense methods to achieve improved results. Furthermore, the proposal has the potential to be extended to other common machine learning attacks, such as the model-robustness challenge, for which we present an analysis framework that helps to identify the conditions under which successful attacks can occur, thereby guiding the creation of preventive patterns that reduce the likelihood of such attacks. Our approach has the versatility to be applied to any situation where multiple attack scenarios exist, potentially leading to significant implications for the field of adversarial learning. Similar techniques may also find applications in advanced methods like federated learning, multi-agent systems, or the analysis of ecosystem robustness. Lastly, the proposal has the practical benefit of minimizing additional computational costs, thereby facilitating its integration into existing training pipelines. Improvements to the code will be made available on the repositories of the DeepMNISTv2 and CIFAR-10 datasets used in this study. Future research will focus on the robustness challenge, where the goal is to create instances that simultaneously test the robustness of both the model and the defense mechanisms. This challenge is particularly significant, as the interplay between these two components is currently poorly understood, thus providing a clear research direction for these studies. One of the major obstacles in dense matching lies in creating a suitable descriptor that can withstand challenges such as illumination changes, distortions, and disruptions.  Recent studies have focused on multibaseline stereoscopy as a way to obtain high-quality matching results.  Although multibaseline models can improve matching accuracy, they can also cause inconsistent results and bridging.  A new method for dense matching based on normal distribution matching has been proposed in this paper.  The method starts with computing the normal distribution transformation of a pixel's color and texture features, then utilizing a collaborative attention model to generate a one-dimensional feature map where similar features from all images are grouped together.  The resulting one-dimensional feature maps from all images are then merged and processed through a self-attention model to produce the final dense matching map.  The new method overcomes some of the limitations of traditional dense matching methods, such as those that are sensitive to light or distorted or lacking a unified axis of reference.  The method has also been adapted for multibaseline stereoscopy by merging the normal distribution transformations from all images before feeding them into the one-dimensional extraction model. In this research, we have evaluated multiple LSTM variants for predictive modeling in music generation, analyzing their performance in generating complete Baroque chorale melodies within a specified context. The variants examined were: (a) vanilla LSTMs, (b) LSTMs with peepholes, (c) LSTms with orthogonality constraints, (d) LSTMs with cellular neural network incidence matrices, and (e) LSTMs with gated feedback connections. Our empirical evaluation has been conducted using a structured dataset of 603 Chorale Progressions from Johann Pachelbel, tested across multiple, sustained look-ahead periods (LAP). Nonetheless, our research shows that LSTMs can successfully model music sequences up to 5 notes ahead. This research presents a novel distributed method for visual object detection using deep Convolutional Neural Networks, which utilizes a camera-equipped Unmanned Aerial Vehicle to identify objects while navigating pre-defined routes. Furthermore, this approach incorporates a weighted decision mechanism to achieve consensus among agents and pinpoint the object's location and trajectory. Our framework incorporates a communication protocol that enables agents to share their detection results, leading to a more accurate and collaborative approach to visual object detection. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through comprehensive indoor and outdoor experiments using a UAV equipped with the SqueezeSegV network, which enables it to achieve an accurate detection rate of 85%, 82%, and 68% for cars, people, and bicycles, respectively. Our results highlight the superiority of our method in pinpointing the object's location and trajectory, with an accuracy of 99%, 100%, and 98% for cars, people, and bicycles, respectively. AOMs) play a crucial role in quantum communication and quantum information systems. They can be utilized to manipulate light pulses across the entire spectrum using radio frequency waves. However, the AOM system's quantum reliability relies on minimizing the impact of unwanted optical background noise arising from the standing wave created by the radio frequency and the optical pulse. In this context, a novel international collaboration has observed a significant effect of this noise on the optical pulse, specifically its amplitude and phase. Notably, the magnitude of this noise is influenced by the radio frequency power and can be largely mitigated by aligning the AOM in a particular direction. This noise mechanism is a major obstacle that could impede the development of quantum optical systems, and thus understanding its origin, other potential issues, and contributing factors is vital for creating reliable quantum optical systems. Although the observed noise has a distinct acoustic origin, the factors contributing to this noise are still uncertain and require further investigation. In this study, the authors have primarily addressed the noise arising from the AOM system. In an accompanying manuscript, the authors present another experiment involving an opto-acoustic interaction in a fibre loop, where the acoustic field is closely integrated with the optical pulse. The observed noise in this experiment has several distinct characteristics, possibly originating from the opto-acoustic interaction. The authors have made some preliminary assumptions regarding the factors contributing to this noise and have demonstrated that minimizing the impact of this noise is essential for quantum optical systems, particularly when the radio frequency power is high. In light of these findings, the authors have introduced a new method for mitigating the noise by using a controlled opto-acoustic field inside a fibre loop. This demonstration has shown that it is feasible to obtain a quantum state with minimal background noise, thereby enhancing the quantum optical system's performance. ients (FXTs) are thought to originate from either supernovae or neutron star activity and serve as potential targets for detecting electromagnetic signals associated with gravitational waves via dedicated sky surveys. Despite FXTs being a valuable source of gravitational waves, a significant limitation in current analysis methods prevents full utilization of their temporal properties, causing many events to be incorrectly classified as background noise. We address this issue with a spectral clustering algorithm that is capable of leveraging temporal information in FXTs. Our analysis was performed using 52 FXTs from a recent sky survey, and the resulting classification produced 53 stable classifications, surpassing the number of previous classifications obtained with traditional methods. Of these, 11 FXTs were initially misclassified by the original analysis, highlighting the efficacy of our approach in accurately analyzing FXTs, regardless of their origin. Even if remotes can collect users' sensory inputs such as video, audio, and sentiment, labeling these sensory inputs with relevant features is a considerable challenge.  To overcome this, we introduce two innovative methods to analyze sensory inputs: (1) an edge-based data augmentation technique that uses linear transformations to enhance low-quality sensory inputs and increases training dataset size; and (2) an online transfer learning method that utilizes sensory inputs collected during streaming to transfer knowledge from one ML model to another, improving its performance and accuracy. We intend to share our implementations via open-source software to facilitate the development of ML models that predict quality of experience from sensory inputs. To address this challenge, deep learning has been employed, with techniques such as network architectures and training strategies being explored. However, the limited transferability of these models and their training strategies poses a significant concern for clinical applications. To overcome this limitation, a novel method is proposed to enhance the generalizability of MRI reconstruction models. This method, known as distributed learning, allows multiple sites to train a deep learning model collaboratively from local data, unlocking the potential for scalable model development. To demonstrate its effectiveness, a distributed learning framework is designed for k-space data reconstruction and tested using numerical simulations with varied imaging parameters. Notably, the proposed framework produces comparable image quality compared to a model trained on comprehensive data, outperforming a model without distributed learning. Importantly, the results reveal that distributed learning models can successfully translate to unseen data, ex vivo and in vivo scans, and imaging modalities with minimal adjustments to the framework. To facilitate its adoption, the source code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available. Based on these findings, distributed learning appears to be a promising method for developing versatile and multi-faceted MRI reconstruction models. Despite its popularity, online PCA methods often suffer from the limitations of outdated components continuously being incorporated into the model, leading to decreased performance over time. This problem is specifically observed in online incremental learning where successive models are stacked to accumulate knowledge for improved overall classification. In an attempt to overcome this issue, this paper introduces a universal framework for updating online PCA without discarding previous features. Therefore, the proposed model retains all learned features from previous time points and seamlessly integrates them with model updates from the current epoch. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method's superiority over several state-of-the-art online PCA approaches.
