However, the criteria used to gauge a module's adaptability are often unclear, and conventional evaluation methods may lead to overemphasizing fit measures like accuracy and negative log-likelihood at the expense of disruptive optimization practices. To shed light on this underdevelopment, we introduce a novel approach to assessing the versatility of a neural network module. Inspired by the idea that a general module should be applicable across diverse datasets, we propose training the module on a collection of datasets simultaneously, rather than on a single dataset. By following this framework, we are able to identify a specific module, known as the Gaussian kernel module, which can be used in convolutional neural networks to achieve impressive results, including achieving an 83.0% top-5 accuracy on the ImageNet dataset with only 0.8M parameters. Our work also analyzes the impact of model sparsity on robustness, and we achieve a sparsity rate of 95.0% without compromising the network's performance. Ultimately, the evaluation framework developed in this research seeks to promote the development of versatile neural network modules.   We also explore extensions of our main result, particularly focusing on the minimum multi-partition covering problem and the maximum multi-partition vertex covering problem. To address these challenges, we develop a mesh-free approach based on the moving-kernels framework, implementing two novel discretization schemes for the nonlinear Euler-Lenz equations and adapting existing mesh-free methods for the modified Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations. A mesh convergence study is conducted, and the proposed methods are validated through both 2D and 3D numerical simulations of various electric double layer scenarios. To enhance convergence rates, we introduce a final scheme for the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations. Furthermore, we use the moving-kernels approach to derive mesh-free formulations for the nonlinear Euler-Lenz and Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations in multiple materials. This mesh-free framework provides a natural extension of classical mesh-based methods and serves as a continuous approximation of the Lagrange formulation. As far as we know, this mesh-free framework is the first of its kind to address both nonlinear ionic transport and electrostatic interactions. It requires only the integration of kernel functions and material properties at arbitrary points, making it a computationally efficient approach. To demonstrate its potential, we have conducted a few illustrative examples of both 2D and 3D multiple material simulations, showcasing its properties and shortcomings. To facilitate future research, we have provided the code used in this paper on GitHub, with the prefix 'MK-PNP-EL' identifying the mesh-free formulations used in this work. However, the code for the final scheme of the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations is still in development and will be made available in a subsequent update. As for the mesh-free formulation of the nonlinear Euler-Lenz equations, we have completed the work but have not yet performed any stability analysis. This is an area that we plan to tackle in a future research study. To conclude, the results of this work have significant potential in various applications and can be extended to other areas, such as the Corpart-Poiseuille-Overbeck model, which describes time-dependent ionic transport. This is an area that we plan to tackle in a future research study and is therefore 'work in progress'. However, the limited number of images available in public datasets hinders deep learning research for this specific task. To overcome this issue, we have created a comprehensive dataset of CT scans from patients with suspected ILD and COPD, as well as healthy individuals, to facilitate accurate detection of abnormal airway dilatation. Our dataset contains 229,792 images divided into four categories, totaling 8.8 million segments, each annotated by radiologists to facilitate the supervision of deep learning models. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we have conducted cross-validation experiments using various deep learning architectures, achieving the lowest loss on validation segments among all datasets and significantly outperforming standard CNNs with dropout. Additionally, we have found that ensembling different models can yield enhanced performance compared to using a single deep learning model. Furthermore, we observed consistent results when testing models on both CT scan images and individual segments, although we found that validating certain architectures solely on images failed to reproduce the same performance as validating on segments. Our dataset is accessible online at https://github.com/nghuythinh/SUAS-CT.
